Two vectors of one disease, both found by MM-241 testing: the wallet's per-identity DID-doc cache expects the **PLC data shape** (\`{did, alsoKnownAs, rotationKeys, verificationMethods, services}\`) — its readers are the home card's custody badge (\`rotationKeys[0]\`) and \`extractPdsFromPlcDoc\` — but three flows were refreshing it with the **W3C document**, which carries no \`rotationKeys\`:

- **[MM-301](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-301/claim-flow-caches-empty-rotationkeys-w3c-doc-parse-migrate-button)**: \`claim::submit_claim\` re-fetched via \`discover_pds\`, whose \`PlcDidDocument.rotation_keys\` is empty by construction from the W3C parse → the claimed bsky identity on the phone cached \`rotationKeys: []\`, so the **\"Migrate to another PDS\" entry** (gated on \`rotationKeys[0] == device key\`) never appeared — blocking MM-241 leg (b).

- New \`PdsClient::fetch_plc_data_document\` (\`GET /{did}/data\`) is the single canonical cache-refresh fetch; **claim, migrate, and recovery** all use it (no more hand-rolled W3C fetches).

Stale caches repair on the next home load — no re-claiming, no user action.

What shipped in the second commit:
- **One canonical fetch**: `PdsClient::fetch_plc_data_document` (`GET /{did}/data`) replaces three hand-rolled W3C fetches — claim, migrate, and recovery all cache the PLC data shape now, so this bug class can't recur per-flow.
- **The self-heal that fixes your phone**: a new `refresh_did_doc` command, invoked automatically by the home screen whenever a cached doc lacks `rotationKeys`. First home load on the new build → your bsky identity's cache repairs from plc.directory → badge flips to "Root key" → the **Migrate to another PDS** button appears. No re-claiming.
- Also caught and fixed a test my MM-300 commit had silently broken: the orchestrator's ignored full-pipeline test still mocked the old endpoint, and my earlier `migrate` filter didn't match `migration_…` — it's on `/data` now and passes. (The only remaining ignored failures require a live localhost Custos; pre-existing, unrelated.)

Verification: 343 wallet Rust tests + the mock-based ignored tests, clippy `-D warnings`, fmt, `pnpm check` (0 errors), and 64 vitest tests — all clean.

**Path to leg (b) from here:**
1. Merge #202 → TestFlight builds automatically (I'll watch it as usual).
2. Install on your phone, open the app — confirm the bsky identity now shows "Root key" and the migrate button.
3. Leg (b): destination `https://ezpds-staging.up.railway.app` + a staging claim code, OAuth against bsky as source. Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/pr-review-comments

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

## Fetch unresolved threads

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line
          comments(first:30){nodes{author{login} body url}}
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F pr=<number> \
| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

The PR is ready for your merge whenever CodeRabbit's re-review settles — then the TestFlight build with MM-300+301 is what puts the migrate button on your phone for leg (b).

hm, merged and got the latest testflight on my device. when I sign in to my current pds, the bsky pds screen shows with an authorize screen requesting an oauth token as far as I can see. Shouldn't I be getting a login screen requesting that I input my username and password?

Yes — that's exactly right, and it's the deliberate design difference between the two flows:

- **The claim flow (leg a)** used a username/password login screen inside the app, because its next steps were PLC identity operations (`requestPlcOperationSignature`/`signPlcOperation`) that bsky.social only permits with a full session — no OAuth token a third-party app can obtain grants those (that was the whole MM-289 saga, ADR-0021).
- **The outbound migration flow (leg b)** doesn't need any identity operation from bsky — the PLC op is **self-signed by your phone's Secure Enclave key**, which is the entire point of what you're about to prove. All it needs from bsky as source is repo export, blob fetch, preferences, service auth, and the final deactivate — all covered by a standard OAuth grant (`transition:generic`). So the source login is the in-app OAuth sheet (ASWebAuthenticationSession), not a password form.

As for why you jumped straight to the *authorize* page without typing credentials: the OAuth sheet shares Safari's cookie jar, so if you've signed into bsky.social in Safari before (including during earlier testing), bsky recognizes the session and skips its login form, going directly to consent. If you'd never logged in there, you'd see bsky's own username/password page first, then this same consent screen.

Two quick checks before you tap Authorize:

1. **The account named on the consent page is `malpercio-obsign.bsky.social`** — if Safari's cookie is for a different bsky account, the flow would authorize the wrong one (the orchestrator does re-check the DID matches the migration, so a mismatch fails safely, but better to catch it at the screen).
2. The requesting app should identify as the wallet (the canonical `identitywallet.obsign.org` client).

Then authorize and let it run: destination `https://ezpds-staging.up.railway.app` + your staging claim code. The pipeline from there is the one leg (r) already proved — the only new seam is bsky-as-source honoring `transition:generic` on `getServiceAuth`, preferences export, and `deactivateAccount`. If it trips, the unified-log line will name the seam, same drill as always.

Full picture, cleanly reproduced and probes revoked:

| Credential tier | `getServiceAuth` for `createAccount` |
|---|---|
| Full session (password `createSession`) | ✅ mints |
| **Privileged** app password | ✅ mints |
| Plain app password / **OAuth `transition:generic`** ← your phone | ❌ `insufficient access` |

So bsky gates minting a `createAccount` service token at the **privileged** tier, and the wallet's outbound source login sits below it. This is MM-289's sibling: the orchestrator's design assumed `transition:generic` covers everything a *self-signed* migration needs from the source — true for repo/blobs/preferences/deactivate, false for this one mint. Leg (r) couldn't catch it because Custos's `require_rpc` is laxer than the reference and lets `transition:generic` mint any method (an MM-292-family divergence that masked the wall).

Filing the ticket with this evidence. On the fix, two real options:

1. **Password source login for outbound migration** (my recommendation): swap `prepare_source_auth`/`complete_source_auth` OAuth for the claim flow's password `createSession` machinery (`authenticate_source_pds` already exists, with 2FA handling and the HTTPS/account-match guards). Consistent with ADR-0021's logic — migrating away is exactly the class of account-authority operation the reference gates behind a real session. Honest UX: "sign in with your password to move your account." Works identically against bsky and Custos sources, so legs (b)/(c)/(d) all use one path.
2. **Request `transition:chat.bsky` in the OAuth scope** to reach the privileged tier — technically works, but semantically absurd (asking for DM access to migrate) and fragile against future reference changes. I'd reject it.

Option 1 touches the migration flow's auth step end to end (backend command swap + the source-auth screen becomes a password screen, mirroring `PdsAuthScreen`), plus an ADR-0021 amendment noting migration joins the claim flow on the password path — and then a new TestFlight build. Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/use-railway

# Use Railway

## Railway resource model

Railway organizes infrastructure in a hierarchy:

- **Workspace** is the billing and team scope. A user belongs to one or more workspaces.
- **Project** is a collection of services under one workspace. It maps to one deployable unit of work.
- **Environment** is an isolated configuration plane inside a project (for example, `production`, `staging`). Each environment has its own variables, config, and deployment history.
- **Service** is a single deployable unit inside a project. It can be an app from a repo, a Docker image, or a managed database.
- **Bucket** is an S3-compatible object storage resource inside a project. Buckets are created at the project level and deployed to environments. Each bucket has credentials (endpoint, access key, secret key) for S3-compatible access.
- **Deployment** is a point-in-time release of a service in an environment. It has build logs, runtime logs, and a status lifecycle.

Most CLI commands operate on the linked project/environment/service context. Use `railway status --json` to see the context, and `--project`, `--environment`, `--service` flags to override.

## Tool routing

Railway has three agent-facing operation paths. Choose the path that matches the job:

- **Railway CLI** (`railway`): workflows that depend on local machine state such as current working directory deploys, `railway up`, `railway run`, SSH, database analysis scripts, local linking, interactive setup, or exact command output.
- **Remote MCP** (`https://mcp.railway.com`): default plugin MCP path for account/project/service discovery, deployment state, bounded logs, feature flags, simple redeploys, simple project creation, or complex Railway workflows that can be handed to `railway-agent`. Remote MCP uses Railway OAuth and does not depend on local CLI state.
- **GraphQL**: operations that neither MCP nor CLI exposes, or when a reference gives a specific GraphQL fallback.

If multiple paths are available, choose the one that preserves the needed context. The CLI fits workflows that need the current repo, local credentials, SSH, database scripts, or exact command output. Remote MCP fits OAuth-scoped platform operations that do not need local files or CLI state.

Optional: if the current agent already has a user-installed local CLI MCP (`railway mcp`) configured, it can be used for CLI-backed platform operations not yet exposed by remote MCP. Published plugin configs do not install or launch local CLI MCP.

Use `scripts/railway-api.sh` for GraphQL only when neither MCP nor CLI exposes the operation, or when a reference gives a specific GraphQL fallback.

## Parsing Railway URLs

Users often paste Railway dashboard URLs. Extract IDs before doing anything else:

```
https://railway.com/project/<PROJECT_ID>/service/<SERVICE_ID>?environmentId=<ENV_ID>
https://railway.com/project/<PROJECT_ID>/service/<SERVICE_ID>
```

The URL always contains `projectId` and `serviceId`. It may contain `environmentId` as a query parameter. If the environment ID is missing and the user specifies an environment by name (e.g., "production"), resolve it:

```bash
scripts/railway-api.sh \
  'query getProject($id: String!) {
    project(id: $id) {
      environments { edges { node { id name } } }
    }
  }' \
  '{"id": "<PROJECT_ID>"}'
```

Match the environment name (case-insensitive) to get the `environmentId`.

**Prefer passing explicit IDs** to CLI commands (`--project`, `--environment`, `--service`) and scripts (`--project-id`, `--environment-id`, `--service-id`) instead of running `railway link`. This avoids modifying global state and is faster.

## Intent-based routing

Route by user intent *before* running preflight checks. The preflight ceremony below is for diagnostic and configuration work — it adds friction when the user just wants to ship something or sign up.

**Deploy-from-cwd intent** ("deploy", "ship", "push to Railway", "deploy this app"):
- Skip the `railway whoami` / `railway status` preflights.
- Run `railway up` directly — it self-validates auth, signs the user in (the CLI opens a browser) if they're unauthenticated, and chains into project + service creation and deploy.
- Announce intent before invoking: *"Running `railway up` — it'll sign you in if needed and deploy this directory."*
- **Do NOT ask the user to run `railway login` first.** The chain handles auth as part of the deploy.
- If the environment can't open a browser, the CLI prints a device-code sign-in link and waits — follow [Device-code sign-in: relay the link immediately](#account-creation--sign-in) (run in background, relay the link to the user the moment it prints).

**Signup intent** ("sign me up", "create my Railway account", "register me", "get me on Railway"):
- **If the current directory has a deployable app (e.g. `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, `go.mod`, `Dockerfile`, source to build), run `railway up`** — it signs the user up *and* deploys in one shot, landing them on a running app. A detected agent harness authorizes the project creation, so **bare `railway up` is enough** — there's no extra prompt to clear. Use it even when the user only said "sign me up": shipping their app is the goal, so don't make them pick a command and don't drop to a bare login. For scripted or agent runs, `railway up -y` is the robust form — it skips prompts and forces the create non-interactively even if harness detection misses. `railway login` is NOT the default for signup when there's something to deploy.
- **Only when there is nothing to deploy** — an empty / non-app directory, or the user explicitly says they just want an account with no deploy — use `railway login` (creates new accounts on the fly through the same OAuth surface). There is no separate signup command.
- Signup is the flow most likely to hit the device-code wait (brand-new users in sandboxed/headless agent environments). Follow [Device-code sign-in: relay the link immediately](#account-creation--sign-in) — a signup lost to an expired code is a lost user, not a retry.

**Sandbox / remote-build intent** ("give me a sandbox", "spin up a scratch environment", "build this remotely", "run this remotely", "checkpoint/snapshot the sandbox", "save this sandbox state", "restore my sandbox"):
- Load [sandbox.md](references/sandbox.md) and follow it. Sandboxes require the feature to be enabled in Priority Boarding — if a sandbox command fails with a feature-availability error, prompt the user to enable Sandboxes in Priority Boarding rather than retrying.

**Other intents** (querying state, listing projects, configuring variables, debugging failures):
- Follow the Preflight section below.

## Preflight

Before any mutation, verify the tool path and context:

```bash
command -v railway                # CLI installed
RAILWAY_CALLER="skill:use-railway@1.3.5" RAILWAY_AGENT_SESSION="railway-skill-$(date +%s)-$$" railway whoami --json
railway --version                 # check CLI version
```

**Exception**: `railway up` and `railway login` self-validate auth and run their own unauth-aware flows. Don't run `railway whoami` before them — it adds a redundant failing call without changing what you do next. See [Account creation & sign-in](#account-creation--sign-in).

### Skill freshness

Once per session, alongside the preflight checks, verify the installed Railway agent tooling is current. Root help ends with an `Agent tooling:` health section (printed to stderr, CLI 5.9+; older CLIs print nothing — skip this check rather than retrying):

```bash
railway --help 2>&1 | grep -A4 "Agent tooling:"
```

Act on what it reports:

- Skills installed and up to date — continue; nothing to do.
- An update is available (`rev <a> → <b> available`) — run `railway skills update`, then tell the user to restart their coding tool so the updated skills load. This session keeps running on the old skill revision until restart: finish the current request, and if this skill's guidance disagrees with the updated CLI's own output, trust the CLI.
- Skills or MCP server missing (`✗` lines) — run `railway setup agent -y`, then tell the user to restart their coding tool.

Check once per session and don't re-run it after acting; the restart prompt to the user is the resolution, not another check.

When Railway MCP is available and the job is a platform-state read, use the matching MCP read instead of shelling out. If using the CLI path, run the CLI checks above.

For Railway CLI calls made while this skill is active, prefix the command with `RAILWAY_CALLER=skill:use-railway@1.3.5` and a stable `RAILWAY_AGENT_SESSION` reused for the current user request. Generate the session id once per user request, then reuse that exact value for later Railway CLI calls in the same workflow. Do not run a separate `export` preflight solely for telemetry; inline env prefixes keep the shell output concise and avoid leaking setup steps into every response.

**Context resolution - URL IDs always win:**
- If the user provides a Railway URL, extract IDs from it. Do NOT run `railway status --json`; it returns the locally linked project, which is usually unrelated.
- If no URL is given, fall back to `railway status --json` for the linked project/environment/service.
- When using MCP tools after resolving local context with `railway status --json`, pass the resolved project, environment, and service IDs explicitly. Do not rely on MCP implicit linked context; MCP may not share the CLI's current working directory link.

If the CLI is missing, guide the user to install it.

```bash
curl -fsSL agents.railway.com | sh # Install CLI and configure detected agents
bash <(curl -fsSL https://railway.com/install.sh) --agents -y # Install CLI and configure detected agents
bash <(curl -fsSL https://railway.com/install.sh) # Shell script (macOS, Linux, Windows via WSL)
npm i -g @railway/cli # npm (macOS, Linux, Windows). Requires Node.js version 16 or higher.
brew install railway # Homebrew (macOS)
```

If not authenticated, see [Account creation & sign-in](#account-creation--sign-in) below — the CLI offers unauthed `railway up` (deploy + sign up/in in one shot) or `railway login` (sign up/in only; new accounts created on the fly). If not linked and no URL was provided, run `railway link --project <id-or-name>`.

If a command is not recognized (for example, `railway environment edit`), the CLI may be outdated. Upgrade with:

```bash
railway upgrade
```

## Account creation & sign-in

Railway uses a single unified OAuth flow for both sign-in and sign-up. The backend detects fresh accounts from durable compliance state (a CLI client that hasn't accepted ToS / Fair Use yet) and adapts the consent screen and post-auth landing page — new users land on a "Welcome to Railway!" page, existing users see the standard confirmation. The CLI does not declare signup intent up front.

Two commands surface this flow, depending on intent:

| Command | When to use |
|---|---|
| `railway up` | Agent-friendly onboarding from the current directory. Unauthenticated → opens the browser (or device-code) to sign in / sign up. With no linked project, a detected agent harness (or `-y`) auto-creates a project + service and deploys; an interactive human is offered create / link-existing / cancel. Add `-y` to skip prompts and force the create non-interactively (works even if harness detection misses). |
| `railway login` | Sign in — *and* sign up. New accounts are created on the fly through the same OAuth surface; there is no separate signup command. |

Related: `railway up --new` creates a *fresh* project + service from the current directory and deploys it even if one is already linked (use when already signed in and the user wants a new app); `--name <name>` overrides the project name.

**Choosing the path:**

- Deploy from cwd → run `railway up` (interactive) or `railway up -y` (skips the confirm prompt). Run it yourself; don't ask the user to sign in separately first.
- New project from cwd when already signed in → `railway up --new`.
- **Sign up with a deployable app in cwd → `railway up`** (signs up *and* deploys — bare `up` works for a detected agent, even if the user only said "sign me up"; add `-y` to skip prompts / force it non-interactively). Sign in, or sign up with nothing to deploy → `railway login` (creates new accounts on the fly).

**Headless / no browser:**

The CLI **auto-detects** SSH sessions, CI, and a missing `DISPLAY` and switches to the device-code flow on its own — you almost never need to force it.

**Do NOT pass `--browserless` just because you are an agent or your shell is non-interactive.** If the human is at this machine (a local IDE or desktop session — the common case), bare `railway login` opens *their* browser directly, which completes far more reliably than relaying a device code (~90% vs ~60% success for agent-driven sign-ins). Being a coding agent does not make the machine headless.

```bash
railway login --browserless   # ONLY for machines with genuinely no browser
```

Forces the device-code flow (RFC 8628): prints a sign-in link and a short code for the user to open on any device. Reserve it for machines where no browser exists — SSH boxes, containers, remote VMs the auto-detection missed. When you do end up in a device-code flow, follow the relay procedure below: surface the sign-in link to the user the moment it prints.

**Agent harness, human present**: when the CLI detects an agent harness (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, …) with a human at the keyboard, `railway up` opens the browser and skips the confirm prompt — the agent invocation is treated as consent. A real human still has to complete OAuth in the browser.

**Device-code sign-in: relay the link immediately (CRITICAL):**

When the CLI can't open a browser (sandboxed shell, container, SSH, no `DISPLAY`), unauthed `railway up` and `railway login` print a sign-in URL + short code and then **block, polling for up to 10 minutes** while the user completes sign-in. The code expires after 10 minutes. If you run this as a normal foreground command, your harness buffers the output until the command exits — **the user never sees the link until the code is already dead**. This is the #1 cause of failed agent-driven signups. Handle it like this:

1. **Preferred — background execution** (e.g. Claude Code: `run_in_background`, then poll with `BashOutput`):
   - Start the command in the background.
   - Poll its output. The instant a sign-in block appears (`Sign in with one click: <url>` on newer CLIs, or `Sign in at: <url>` / `Enter this code: <code>` on older ones), **stop everything and relay it to the user verbatim** — do not summarize, shorten, or defer it. Prefer the one-click URL when present; otherwise relay the URL and code together. Tell the user to open the link now.
   - Leave the command running and keep polling. When the user completes sign-in, the same process picks up the session and continues into the deploy on its own. Then verify per the deploy rules below.
2. **No background support — set expectations, use the longest timeout:**
   - Before running, tell the user: *"This will print a sign-in link — I'll show it to you the moment I have it. Please complete it promptly; the code expires in 10 minutes."*
   - Run with the longest timeout your harness allows.
   - If the command times out or is killed before sign-in completed, the printed code is **no longer being monitored** — a late click does nothing. Relay whatever link appeared anyway for context, then immediately re-run the command and relay the **new** link, telling the user to always use the newest one.
3. **Never** wait silently for the command to finish before showing the link, and never report the sign-in as failed without first relaying the link and giving the user a chance to act.

The browser transport needs none of this — the CLI opens the browser on the user's machine itself.

**JSON / CI modes do not auto-prompt**: `railway up --json` and `railway up --ci` will NOT open a browser for an unauthed user. `--json` emits a structured error instead:

```json
{"error":"Not signed in.","code":"NOT_AUTHENTICATED","hint":"Run `railway login` to authenticate, then re-run."}
```

When you see `code: NOT_AUTHENTICATED`, authenticate the user with `railway login`, then retry the original command.

**Fully unattended (no human at all)**: set `RAILWAY_API_TOKEN` (account-scoped) or `RAILWAY_TOKEN` (project-scoped) instead of running an interactive login. A brand-new user with no token and no human present cannot complete signup — there is no headless account-creation path.

## Agent tooling

Use direct Railway CLI commands for deterministic operations. Use `railway agent` only when the user explicitly asks for Railway Agent, wants a natural-language investigation, or the task is broader than a single resource operation.

Set up Railway skills, MCP, and authentication with:

```bash
railway setup agent
railway setup agent -y
railway setup agent --remote
```

`railway setup agent -y` skips the interactive login flow. If the user isn't authenticated after setup, run `railway login`.

Install or update MCP and skills directly when the user names a target tool:

```bash
railway mcp install --remote
railway mcp install --agent codex --remote
railway mcp install --agent cursor --remote
railway skills
railway skills update --agent codex
railway skills remove --agent cursor
```

Supported targets include `claude-code`, `cursor`, `codex`, `opencode`, `copilot`, and `factory-droid`. The `--remote` flag configures `https://mcp.railway.com` instead of a local `railway mcp` stdio server.

Use Railway Agent chat with:

```bash
railway agent
railway agent -p "why is my service crashing?"
railway agent -p "summarize the deployment status" --json
railway agent --list --json
railway agent --thread-id <thread-id>
```

`railway agent` requires user OAuth authentication from `railway login`. Project tokens (`RAILWAY_TOKEN`) are not supported for Railway Agent chat. If an agent command is unavailable, upgrade with `railway upgrade --yes`.

## Common quick operations

These are frequent enough to handle without loading a reference. Use the matching MCP tool when the job is platform-scoped and the tool is available; otherwise use the CLI:

```bash
railway status --json                                    # current context
railway whoami --json                                    # auth and workspace info
railway project list --json                              # list projects
railway service list --json                              # services in current environment (verify before retrying `add`)
railway add --database <type> --json                     # add one database; ALWAYS pass --json
railway add --service <name> --json                      # add empty service; ALWAYS pass --json
railway variable list --service <svc> --json             # list variables
railway variable set KEY=value --service <svc>           # set a variable
railway domain list --service <svc> --json               # domains and DNS status
railway logs --service <svc> --lines 200 --json          # recent logs
railway logs --service <svc> --network --lines 200 --json # network flow snapshot
railway metrics --service <svc> --since 1h --json        # resource and HTTP metrics summary
railway up --detach -m "<summary>"                       # deploy current directory (returns at QUEUED — verify before reporting)
railway deployment list --json                           # poll newest deployment status after a detached up
railway bucket list --json                               # list buckets in current environment
railway bucket info --bucket <name> --json               # bucket storage and object count
railway bucket credentials --bucket <name> --json        # S3-compatible credentials
```

## Routing

For anything beyond quick operations, load the reference that matches the user's intent. Load only what you need, one reference is usually enough, two at most.

| Intent | Reference | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| **Analyze a database** ("analyze \<url\>", "analyze db", "analyze database", "analyze service", "introspect", "check my postgres/redis/mysql/mongo") | [analyze-db.md](references/analyze-db.md) | Database introspection and performance analysis. analyze-db.md directs you to the DB-specific reference. **This takes priority over the status/operate routes when a Railway URL to a database service is provided alongside "analyze".** |
| Create or connect resources | [setup.md](references/setup.md) | Projects, services, databases, buckets, templates, workspaces |
| Ship code or manage releases | [deploy.md](references/deploy.md) | Deploy, redeploy, restart, build config, monorepo, Dockerfile |
| Change configuration | [configure.md](references/configure.md) | Environments, variables, config patches, domains, networking |
| Manage feature flags | [feature-flags.md](references/feature-flags.md) | List/create/update project flags via MCP; workspace flags read-only; SDK runtime reads |
| Define or import project configuration as code ("IaC", "infrastructure as code", ".railway/railway.ts", "config plan/apply/pull") | [iac.md](references/iac.md) | Project-level Railway configuration files, import, plan, apply, drift checks, destructive apply safety |
| Check health or debug failures | [operate.md](references/operate.md) | Status, logs, metrics, build/runtime triage, recovery |
| Use a sandbox or build remotely ("sandbox", "scratch environment", "ephemeral box", "build remotely", "remote build", "run this remotely", "checkpoint", "snapshot/save/restore sandbox state") | [sandbox.md](references/sandbox.md) | Create/fork sandboxes, run commands remotely, remote template builds, checkpoints (save/restore sandbox state), port forwarding, teardown. Requires Sandboxes enabled in Priority Boarding — if unavailable, prompt the user to enable it. |
| Request from API, docs, or community | [request.md](references/request.md) | Railway GraphQL API queries/mutations, metrics queries, Central Station, official docs |

If the request spans two areas (for example, "deploy and then check if it's healthy"), load both references and compose one response.

## Execution rules

1. Use Railway CLI for workflows that need the current repo, local shell, SSH, database scripts, local Railway context, or exact command output.
2. Use Remote MCP for OAuth-scoped platform operations that match an available MCP tool and do not need local files or CLI state.
3. Use local CLI MCP only when the current agent already has it explicitly configured and it exposes a needed operation not available through Remote MCP.
4. Fall back to `scripts/railway-api.sh` for operations neither MCP nor CLI exposes.
5. Use `--json` output where available for reliable parsing.
6. Resolve context before mutation. Know which project, environment, and service you're acting on.
7. For destructive actions (delete service, remove deployment, drop database), confirm intent and state impact before executing.
8. After mutations, verify the result with a read-back command or MCP read.
9. **Never report a deploy as successful without observing a terminal SUCCESS.** `railway up --detach` returning (it prints "Build queued") and a streaming `railway up` cut off by a shell timeout only confirm the build *started*. Poll `railway deployment list --json` with the same `--project`, `--environment`, and `--service` scope used for the deploy until the newest deployment's `status` is `SUCCESS` (report deployed). If status is `FAILED` or `CRASHED`, triage per [operate.md](references/operate.md). If status is `NEEDS_APPROVAL`, `SLEEPING`, `SKIPPED`, `REMOVED`, `REMOVING`, or an unknown value, report the exact state and next action; do not claim success. A streaming `up` that exits on its own is authoritative: exit 0 = deployed, exit 1 = failed.

## User-only commands (NEVER execute directly)

These commands modify database state and require the user to run them directly in their terminal. **Do NOT execute these with Bash. Instead, show the command and ask the user to run it.**

| Command | Why user-only |
|---------|---------------|
| `python3 scripts/enable-pg-stats.py --service <name>` | Modifies shared_preload_libraries, may restart database |
| `python3 scripts/pg-extensions.py --service <name> install <ext>` | Installs database extension |
| `python3 scripts/pg-extensions.py --service <name> uninstall <ext>` | Removes database extension |
| `ALTER SYSTEM SET ...` | Changes PostgreSQL configuration |
| `DROP EXTENSION ...` | Removes database extension |
| `CREATE EXTENSION ...` | Installs database extension |

When these operations are needed:
1. Explain what the command does and any side effects (e.g., restart required)
2. Show the exact command the user must run
3. Wait for user confirmation that they ran it
4. Verify the result with a read-only query

## Composition patterns

Multi-step workflows follow natural chains:

- **Add object storage**: setup (create bucket), setup (get credentials), configure (set S3 variables on app service)
- **First deploy**: setup (create project + service), configure (set variables and source), deploy, operate (verify healthy)
- **Fix a failure**: operate (triage logs), configure (fix config/variables), deploy (redeploy), operate (verify recovery)
- **Add a domain**: configure (add domain + set port), operate (verify DNS and service health)
- **Docs to action**: request (fetch docs answer), route to the relevant operational reference

When composing, return one unified response covering all steps. Don't ask the user to invoke each step separately.

## Setup decision flow

When the user wants to create or deploy something, determine the right action from current context:

1. input.title: verify_service_auth_jwt rejects ES256K — bsky-minted createAccount service tokens fail, blocking inbound migration from reference PDSes
input.description:
## Found by

MM-241 leg (b), on device, first retry after MM-302: the orchestrator now gets past `getServiceAuth` (the password source login works) and fails one step later at `createAccount` on **staging** with `ACCOUNT_CREATION_FAILED` ("Couldn't create the account on the destination PDS").

## Root cause

`crates/pds/src/auth/jwt.rs::verify_service_auth_jwt` hard-requires `alg: ES256` and verifies with `crypto::verify_p256_signature` only. But a reference PDS signs service-auth JWTs with the account's `#atproto` signing key, and on bsky.social that key is **secp256k1** — the token header is `{"typ":"JWT","alg":"ES256K"}`.

Reproduced end-to-end with curl (real bsky full-session → `getServiceAuth?aud=did:web:ezpds-staging.up.railway.app&lxm=com.atproto.server.createAccount` → replay against staging `createAccount`):

```
{"error":{"code":"INVALID_TOKEN","message":"service auth token must be ES256"}}
```

The test account's PLC doc confirms: `verificationMethods.atproto = did:key:zQ3she26...` (zQ3s = secp256k1 multicodec).

`crates/crypto/src/plc.rs` already learned this exact lesson — its `verify_signature` dispatches on the did:key multicodec prefix (P-256 `zDn…` **and** secp256k1 `zQ3…`) precisely because "the reference ecosystem (bsky.social) signs its operations with secp256k1". The JWT verifier never got the same treatment. Leg (r) masked it because Custos-to-Custos service tokens are P-256/ES256.

## Fix (server-side only — no wallet build needed)

In `verify_service_auth_jwt`:
1. Accept `alg: ES256` **or** `ES256K` (still an allowlist — no other algorithms, no `none`).
2. Require the alg to **match the key's curve** (multicodec prefix of the `#atproto` did:key): ES256 ↔ zDn (P-256), ES256K ↔ zQ3s (secp256k1). A mismatch is a downgrade/confusion attempt → reject.
3. The low-S canonicality check currently parses the signature as `p256::ecdsa::Signature` — this must dispatch per curve too (`k256::ecdsa::Signature::normalize_s` for ES256K; atproto requires low-S on both curves).
4. Verify via curve-dispatching verification (crypto crate already has `verify_k256_sec1` / the plc.rs dispatch pattern — expose or mirror it for raw signing-input verification).

Note `mint_service_auth_jwt` stays ES256/P-256 — Custos accounts sign with P-256; only *verification* of foreign tokens needs both curves.

## Sequencing / test-state notes

- The ES256K rejection happens **before** invite-code consumption and before account creation, so failed attempts left no partial state on staging and the claim code is still valid.
- `reserveSigningKey` for the DID **did** succeed on staging (wallet reached createAccount), which is fine — migration-mode createAccount expects it.
- Tests: unit tests minting a K-256-signed token (k256 crate) → verify accepts low-S / rejects high-S / rejects alg-key mismatch (ES256 header + zQ3s key and vice versa).
- Ships via merge to main → staging auto-deploy. Retry leg (b) with the **same** wallet build.

# Linear Development Workflow

This skill manages the full lifecycle of working on a Linear issue: from picking it up through opening a PR.

## Starting Work on an Issue

When the user indicates they want to work on a Linear issue (e.g., "Let's work on MM-42"):

1. **Parse the issue identifier** from the user's message. The pattern is `MM-` followed by a number.

2. **Fetch the issue details** from Linear using the `get_issue` tool with the parsed identifier. Display a brief summary to the user: title, description (truncated if long), priority, and any existing labels.

3. **Update the issue in Linear:**
   - Set the status to **"In Progress"**
   - Assign it to **"me"** (the authenticated user)

   Use the `save_issue` tool with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Progress"`, and `assignee: "me"`.

4. **Create a git branch from a fresh base** using the issue's suggested branch name:
   - The `get_issue` response includes a `branchName` field — use that as the branch name.
   - **Fetch first, then branch from the remote tip — never from a possibly-stale local HEAD:**
     `git fetch origin main && git checkout -b <branchName> origin/main`
     A stale base silently duplicates work that already merged (hours lost rebuilding an already-shipped backend is the known failure mode).
   - If the branch already exists locally, check it out, then run `git log --oneline <branchName>..origin/main` and surface to the user how far behind the base is.

5. **Verify sibling work is in the base.** If the issue depends on or overlaps sibling issues already marked Done in Linear, confirm their PRs are actually present in the branch base (e.g. `git log --oneline origin/main | grep -i mm-nnn`, or check for the files/routes they added) before concluding any related feature is "missing". **"Linear says Done but the code isn't here" is a hard stop-and-verify signal — it almost always means your base is stale, not that the feature needs building.**

6. **Confirm to the user** what happened: issue assigned, status updated, branch created/checked out (and from which base commit). Then ask what they'd like to tackle first, or summarize the issue so they can dive in.

## Opening a PR (Auto-transition to "In Review")

When the user asks to open a PR, create a pull request, or you detect that a PR is being created for a branch associated with a Linear issue:

1. **Identify the Linear issue** from the current branch name. Linear branch names typically contain the issue identifier (e.g., `malpercio/mm-42-fix-the-thing`). Extract the `MM-XXX` portion.

2. **Create the PR** as the user requests (follow normal PR creation workflow).

3. **After the PR is successfully created**, update the Linear issue:
   - Set the status to **"In Review"**
   - Attach the PR URL as a link on the issue using the `links` field in `save_issue`

   Use `save_issue` with the issue's `id`, `state: "In Review"`, and `links: [{"url": "<pr-url>", "title": "Pull Request"}]`.

4. **Confirm** to the user that the issue has been moved to "In Review" and the PR link has been attached.

## Important Notes

- Always fetch the issue first to confirm it exists and get the full `id` (UUID) needed for updates.
- If the issue is already "In Progress" and assigned, skip those updates and just create the branch.
- If branch creation fails (e.g., uncommitted changes), inform the user and suggest next steps rather than silently failing.
- The PR-to-"In Review" transition should happen automatically whenever a PR is opened during a session where the user started work on a Linear issue. Track the active issue identifier throughout the session.

git add Cargo.lock && git commit -m "fix(pds): accept ES256K service-auth JWTs from secp256k1 signing keys (MM-304)

A reference PDS signs service-auth tokens with the account's #atproto
key, which on bsky.social is secp256k1 — the token header is ES256K.
verify_service_auth_jwt hard-required ES256/P-256, so migration-mode
createAccount rejected every bsky-minted token and inbound migration
from the reference ecosystem was impossible (MM-241 leg b). The PLC
verifier learned this lesson long ago (crypto::verify_plc_operation
dispatches both curves); the JWT verifier never did.

- crypto: new verify_did_key_signature (dual-curve dispatch by
  multicodec prefix, per-curve low-S enforcement) and did_key_curve +
  DidKeyCurve for callers that must bind an external algorithm
  identifier to the key material. verify_p256_signature stays
  P-256-only for the admin envelope.
- jwt: alg allowlist becomes ES256 | ES256K, and the declared alg must
  match the #atproto key's actual curve (a mismatched header is

gh pr create --title "fix(pds): accept ES256K service-auth JWTs from secp256k1 signing keys (MM-304)" --body "## Problem

[MM-304](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-304/verify-service-auth-jwt-rejects-es256k-bsky-minted-createaccount) — found by MM-241 leg (b) on device, first retry after MM-302: the wallet now mints the source service token fine, and migration dies one step later at staging's \`createAccount\` with \`ACCOUNT_CREATION_FAILED\`.

A reference PDS signs service-auth JWTs with the account's \`#atproto\` signing key — on bsky.social that key is **secp256k1**, so the token header is \`{\"alg\":\"ES256K\"}\`. \`verify_service_auth_jwt\` hard-required ES256 and verified P-256 only, so every bsky-minted token was rejected:

\`\`\`
{\"error\":{\"code\":\"INVALID_TOKEN\",\"message\":\"service auth token must be ES256\"}}
\`\`\`

\`crypto::verify_plc_operation\` learned this exact lesson already (dual-curve dispatch, because bsky signs PLC ops with secp256k1); the JWT verifier never got the same treatment. Leg (r) masked it — Custos-to-Custos tokens are P-256/ES256.

## Fix

- **crypto**: new \`verify_did_key_signature\` (dual-curve ECDSA-SHA256 dispatch by did:key multicodec prefix, per-curve low-S enforcement — the exact machinery PLC verification uses) plus \`did_key_curve\`/\`DidKeyCurve\` for alg↔key binding. \`verify_p256_signature\` stays deliberately P-256-only for the admin envelope.
- **jwt**: the \`alg\` allowlist becomes **ES256 | ES256K**, and the declared alg must **match the \`#atproto\` key's actual curve** (ES256 ↔ \`zDn…\`, ES256K ↔ \`zQ3s…\`) — a mismatched header is algorithm confusion and is rejected. The hand-rolled low-S pre-check is dropped: it parsed every signature with **p256** scalar arithmetic, which would have checked K-256 signatures against the wrong curve order; the crypto layer enforces low-S against each curve's own order.
- \`mint_service_auth_jwt\` is untouched — Custos signs P-256; only verification of foreign tokens needs both curves.

## Verification

- Unit: ES256K happy path, high-S ES256K rejected (per-curve canonicality), alg↔curve mismatch both directions + non-ECDSA alg rejected. Existing ES256 tests unchanged.
- **End-to-end**: replayed a **real bsky.social-minted ES256K token** (aud = staging's DID) against a local build of this branch configured with staging's server DID: it passes full JWT verification — real secp256k1 signature verified against the key resolved live from plc.directory — and fails only at the expected \`no reserved signing key\` precondition. The same token against deployed staging: rejected at the alg gate.

\`cargo test -p crypto -p pds\`: 84 + 1750 pass. Clippy \`--all-targets -D warnings\`, fmt, lock-check clean.

## Deps

\`k256\` + \`multibase\` added to **pds dev-dependencies only** (workspace-pinned versions already used by \`crypto\`), for minting ES256K test tokens. Production signing stays P-256.

Merging → staging auto-deploy unblocks the MM-241 leg (b) retry with the **same** wallet build." 2>&1 | tail -1

content.text:
Short answer: **no — there's no handle-change surface in the app today, and even the server half is only partially there.** Three layers to it:

**1. The wallet.** The only handle machinery is `registerHandle()` + `HandleRegistrationScreen`, which live in the *create flow* (session-token world, picks a handle on your own PDS during onboarding). Claimed/migrated identities in the `IdentityStore` world — which is what your migrated account is — have no handle UI at all.

**2. Custos.** `com.atproto.identity.updateHandle` exists and works ([update_handle.rs](crates/pds/src/routes/update_handle.rs)): it swaps the handle rows, updates the *locally cached* DID doc, and emits `#identity`. Staging serves `ezpds-staging.up.railway.app` handles (so e.g. `malpercio.ezpds-staging.up.railway.app`), with a DNS-TXT branch for domains you own. But note what it does **not** do: it never submits the `alsoKnownAs` PLC operation to plc.directory. The reference PDS does that automatically, signing with its rotation key. So even after a successful `updateHandle`, the network-visible DID doc still says `at://malpercio-obsign.bsky.social` and bidirectional verification stays broken — the handle change is only locally complete.

**3. The auth wrinkle specific to your migrated account.** `updateHandle` requires a full-access session — and the migration created the staging account with a **NULL password** (the wallet's `createAccount` sends none). So today you can't even `createSession` to call it; you'd have to go through `requestPasswordReset` first, and staging's email sender is the log-only one, meaning fishing the token out of Railway logs. Workable for an operator, not a product.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
This is the sovereignty design meeting its first post-migration lifecycle op. On the reference PDS, "change handle" is one call because the PDS custodies the rotation key and quietly rewrites your PLC doc. In the wallet-sovereign model, the `alsoKnownAs` op should be **device-key-signed** — same as the migration's identity leg — which means the wallet needs a guard variant for it: today's `guard_migration_op` explicitly *requires* `alsoKnownAs` be preserved (and the claim guard forbids all mutation), so a handle op is a third, distinct allowlist: alsoKnownAs may change, keys and services must not.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

So the honest picture: for MM-241 purposes you don't need it (the return leg re-hosts the identity on bsky, which revalidates the handle), but as a product feature "Change handle" is a real gap with three concrete pieces — a per-identity wallet flow (pick served-domain or own-domain handle → `updateHandle` → wallet-signed `alsoKnownAs` PLC op → refresh the cached doc), the missing password/credential story for migrated accounts (set a password during migration, or drive these ops through the wallet's session), and optionally Custos parity with the reference for PDS-custodied accounts.

Want me to file that as a Linear ticket (or a small set — wallet flow, migrated-account credentials, Custos PLC-push parity — they're separable)?
Please do file linear issues

input.description:
## Context

Found after MM-241 leg (b): the migrated identity's handle (`malpercio-obsign.bsky.social`) is now dangling — bsky no longer actively hosts the account, so bidirectional handle verification fails network-wide. The wallet has **no way to change a handle**: `registerHandle()`/`HandleRegistrationScreen` exist only in the create flow (session-token world); claimed/migrated identities in the `IdentityStore` world have no handle surface at all.

## Why this is a distinct guard, not a reuse

On the reference PDS, "change handle" is one call because the PDS custodies the rotation key and rewrites the PLC doc itself. In our sovereign model the `alsoKnownAs` op should be **device-key-signed**, like the migration identity leg. But the existing wallet guards both forbid it:
- `migrate::guard_migration_op` **requires** `alsoKnownAs` preserved (invariant 4)
- the claim guard forbids all mutation except inserting the device key

So this is a third allowlist: **`alsoKnownAs` may change; rotationKeys, verificationMethods, and services must not.**

## Proposed flow (per-identity, from the identity detail screen)

1. Pick the new handle: a served-domain handle from the PDS's `describeServer.availableUserDomains` (staging: `ezpds-staging.up.railway.app`), or a domain the user owns (DNS TXT `_atproto.` verification path).
2. Call `com.atproto.identity.updateHandle` on the hosting PDS (full-access session required — see the migrated-account credential gap ticket).
3. Build + device-key-sign the `alsoKnownAs` PLC op (new `build_handle_op` in `migrate.rs`-style module, with the new guard), submit to plc.directory via the existing `post_plc_operation`.
4. Refresh the cached DID doc (`fetch_plc_data_document`, MM-301 machinery) so the home card updates.

Ordering note: do `updateHandle` first (PDS-side validation/uniqueness), PLC op second; a failure between the two leaves handle resolution ahead of the DID doc, which self-heals on retry.

## Dependencies / siblings

- Requires a full-access session on the hosting PDS — blocked for migrated accounts today (no password; see sibling ticket).
- Custos-side parity for PDS-custodied accounts (updateHandle not pushing the PLC op) is a separate server ticket.

input.title: Migrated accounts land with no password — no credential path to full-access account ops on the destination PDS
input.description:
## Problem

The wallet's outbound migration creates the destination account via service-auth `createAccount` with **no password** (`create_account_migration` sends none; Custos stores NULL — "a migration account may carry no password (OAuth-only)"). After the in-memory Bearer session from the migration is gone (app restart), there is **no way to get a full-access session** on the destination:

- `createSession` — impossible (no password; NULL never verifies)
- OAuth via the wallet's canonical client — the authorize page itself needs the password
- `requestPasswordReset` — works in principle, but staging runs the log-only `LogEmailSender`, so the token lands in Railway logs (operator-only recovery, not a product path)

This blocks every full-access account op on the migrated account: `updateHandle` (MM-305), app passwords, email confirmation/update, `requestPlcOperationSignature`, `deactivateAccount`, `deleteAccount`, agent management…

Concrete instance: `did:plc:u7j7xdhvkwx3xlf6xjkbpdn7` on staging after MM-241 leg (b).

## Options

1. **Set a password during migration** (recommended): the migration flow already collects the *source* password (MM-302's full-session login); add a "set a password for your new server" step (or reuse the create flow's `PasswordScreen` pattern) and include it in `CreateAccountMigrationRequest` — Custos's migration `createAccount` already accepts an optional password (argon2id PHC).
2. **Persist the destination session** the migration mints (Keychain per-DID `oauth-tokens` slot is reserved and unused) so the wallet retains a working session post-migration; still want (1) for recoverability — a session alone can expire/be revoked with no re-entry path.
3. Do both: (1) is the durable credential, (2) is the UX (no re-login right after migrating).

Note the resume path: `create_account_migration` is resumable (MM-299); adding a password to the request must not break the resume branch (which re-issues a session without consuming anything — it ignores the payload beyond the DID, so a differing password on retry is silently ignored; decide whether that's acceptable or the resume should backfill a NULL password).

input.title: Custos updateHandle never submits the alsoKnownAs PLC op — handle changes are locally complete but network-invisible for did:plc accounts
input.description:
## Problem

`routes/update_handle.rs` swaps the local `handles` rows, updates the **locally cached** DID document's `alsoKnownAs` (`db::dids::update_also_known_as`), and emits `#identity` — but never submits a PLC operation to plc.directory. For a `did:plc` account the authoritative DID doc keeps the old handle, so **bidirectional handle verification fails network-wide**: the new handle resolves handle→DID (DNS/well-known), but the DID doc's `alsoKnownAs` doesn't point back. Relays/AppViews show the account handle-invalid.

The reference PDS submits the PLC op itself on handle change, signing with its custodied rotation key.

## Design decision needed (interacts with MM-305)

Custos hosts two kinds of accounts:
- **PDS-custodied** (standard signups whose rotation keys Custos holds, e.g. via the interop path): reference parity applies — `updateHandle` should build + sign + submit the `alsoKnownAs` op with the PDS rotation key, then refresh the cached doc. Machinery exists: `plc_ops.rs` (current-state fetch, op rendering) + `genesis.rs`'s plc.directory POST.
- **Wallet-sovereign** (device key at `rotationKeys[0]`, e.g. migrated-in accounts): the PDS *may* hold a rotation key too (staging's key is in the migrated test account's rotation set), so it *could* sign — but the sovereign design intent is that identity mutations are wallet-signed (MM-305). Decide: does `updateHandle` auto-submit whenever a Custos-held rotation key is in the DID's current rotation set (convenient, reference-parity), or refuse/defer to the wallet flow for sovereign accounts (purist)? Auto-submit is probably right — a handle op doesn't touch keys, and `plc_monitor` on the wallet will see it as a PDS-signed op (check: does the monitor classify a handle-only op signed by a non-device key as an *unauthorized change* alert? If yes, either the wallet flow is the only clean path for sovereign accounts, or the monitor needs to distinguish benign alsoKnownAs-only ops — surface this explicitly rather than shipping alert noise).

## Scope

- Server-side only; no lexicon change (`updateHandle` request/response unchanged).
- Failure ordering: local swap + PLC submit should not be able to half-commit silently — if the PLC POST fails, either roll back the local swap or surface a retryable error state.
- Tests: PDS-custodied happy path (op submitted, cached doc + plc mock agree), sovereign-account behavior per the decision above, PLC-failure path.

Three issues filed, all in the `ezpds` project and cross-linked:

- **[MM-305](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-305/wallet-change-handle-flow-wallet-signed-alsoknownas-plc-op)** (Medium) — the wallet "Change handle" flow: served-domain or own-domain handle picker → `updateHandle` on the hosting PDS → **device-key-signed** `alsoKnownAs` PLC op under a new third guard (alsoKnownAs may change; keys and services must not) → cache refresh. Includes the ordering rationale (PDS first, PLC second, self-healing retry).
- **[MM-306](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-306/migrated-accounts-land-with-no-password-no-credential-path-to-full)** (High) — migrated accounts land with a NULL password and no credential path to full-access ops; this is the blocker in front of MM-305 for your staging account, so I ranked it higher. Recommends collecting a destination password during migration (the server side already accepts one) plus persisting the migration's Bearer session into the reserved per-DID `oauth-tokens` Keychain slot, with a note about the MM-299 resume-path interaction.
- **[MM-307](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-307/custos-updatehandle-never-submits-the-alsoknownas-plc-op-handle)** (Medium) — Custos-side reference parity: `updateHandle` never submits the PLC op, so handle changes are network-invisible for did:plc accounts. Flags the real design fork (auto-submit with a Custos-held rotation key vs. defer to the wallet for sovereign accounts) and a subtle interaction I want to make sure doesn't ship as a surprise: a PDS-signed handle op might trip the wallet's `plc_monitor` as an "unauthorized change" alert, since the monitor classifies by signing key.

Dependency shape: MM-306 → MM-305 (credentials before the wallet flow can call `updateHandle`), MM-307 independent on the server side but its sovereign-account decision should be made together with MM-305. None of them block the MM-241 return leg — migrating back to bsky revalidates the handle on its own.

also -- do we really need a password for the handle change on the custos side? it iterates us further towards a passwordless goal, and the biometric signing of the operation is the proof that the owner is updating the handle

You're right, and it's a sharper design than what I filed. Let me reason it through, because there's one genuine caveat worth pinning:

The handle change has two halves with different trust anchors. The **PLC op** is already fully passwordless — plc.directory verifies the signature against the rotation set, your device key is `rotationKeys[0]`, biometric gates the Enclave. No server credential involved. The **PDS half** (`updateHandle`) can't be *eliminated* — someone has to arbitrate served-domain handle allocation (two DIDs could both write `alice.ezpds-staging...` into their PLC docs; the PDS decides which one it actually serves, enforces uniqueness and reserved names) — but you're right that nothing about that arbitration requires a *password*. It requires proof that the requester owns the DID, and **a device-key signature verified against the DID's current PLC rotation set is strictly stronger proof than a password**. It's also machinery we already have twice over: the admin-companion's signed-request envelope (`auth/guards.rs`, with nonce anti-replay), and MM-304's resolve-DID-doc-then-verify pattern from this very evening.

And the idea generalizes further than the handle: if Custos can verify "this request was signed by a current rotation key of this DID," it can mint a **full session** from that proof — a sovereign, passwordless login to your own PDS. One new endpoint (device-key challenge/signed envelope → session), and *every* full-access account op — handle, email, app passwords, agents, deactivate — works for migrated accounts with zero passwords anywhere. That dissolves MM-306's problem statement entirely: the "no password" state stops being a bug and becomes the intended end state. A password becomes an optional break-glass fallback (device loss recovery is the Shamir story, which already exists), not a requirement.

One honest caveat to record: this makes device-key possession the single credential for the account, so the recovery story has to carry the weight — and note the PDS's own rotation key is in the set too, so "PDS can self-issue sessions" is technically implied, but that grants it nothing it can't already do to data it hosts.

input.title: Sovereign passwordless login — mint a Custos session from a device-key signature over the DID's rotation set (migrated accounts have no password by design)
input.description:
## Reframed (2026-07-12)

Originally filed as "migrated accounts land with no password — set one during migration." **Reframed toward the passwordless goal**: the NULL-password state of a migrated account is the *intended end state*, not a gap. The missing piece is a credential path that matches the sovereignty model — the device key IS the account credential.

## Problem

After outbound migration, the destination account has no password and (post app-restart) no session. Every full-access op is unreachable: `updateHandle` (MM-305), app passwords, email confirm/update, `requestPlcOperationSignature`, `deactivateAccount`, agents management. Concrete instance: `did:plc:u7j7xdhvkwx3xlf6xjkbpdn7` on staging after MM-241 leg (b).

## Design: sovereign session issuance

New Custos endpoint (shape TBD — `POST /v1/sessions/sovereign` or a `createSession` variant): the wallet proves control of the DID by signing a challenge/timestamped envelope with the device key; Custos verifies the signature against the DID's **current PLC rotation set** and issues a full session for the account it hosts under that DID.

Proof of a rotation key is *strictly stronger* than a password — it's the root of the identity. Biometric gating of the Secure Enclave key on-device is the human gate (same model as migration/recovery op signing).

Existing machinery to reuse:
- Signed-request envelope + nonce anti-replay: the admin-device pattern (`auth/guards.rs`, `db/admin_devices.rs` nonce store, `common::ADMIN_TIMESTAMP_WINDOW_SECS`).
- Resolve-DID-doc → verify-against-key: MM-304's `verify_service_auth_jwt` pattern; dual-curve via `crypto::verify_did_key_signature`.

Design points:
- **Which keys qualify:** any key in the DID's current `rotationKeys` is defensible per PLC semantics (rotation key = identity owner). Note this technically includes Custos's own held rotation key — no new power (it already controls hosted data), but document it.
- **Replay/freshness:** nonce or challenge-response; the admin-nonce sweep pattern applies.
- **Wallet side:** persist the issued session in the reserved per-DID `oauth-tokens` Keychain slot; re-login silently via the same signature flow when it expires. Migration's finalize step can do the first sovereign login immediately, so the account is never credential-less.
- **Password becomes optional break-glass** (recoverability if the device is lost is the Shamir/recovery story, which is the wallet's existing responsibility) — not collected during migration by default.

## Why this beats "set a password during migration" (the original proposal)

One mechanism unlocks *all* full-access ops for sovereign accounts, keeps the passwordless product thesis intact, and avoids adding a password prompt to the migration flow that would immediately contradict the pitch ("your keys are your identity").

The handle flow then becomes fully passwordless end to end:

1. Sovereign login (MM-306) → full session, silently, no user credential entry.

input.title: Normalize account emails — Custos matches byte-exact where the reference PDS lowercases
input.description:
## Problem

Account emails are stored verbatim and every lookup is byte-exact (`db::accounts::resolve_by_email`: `WHERE a.email = ?`; same for the uniqueness preflight in `uniqueness.rs` and the `confirmEmail`/`updateEmail` match). The reference PDS lowercases emails on store and lookup. Consequences hit during MM-241: a typo'd/differently-cased email at account creation makes `requestPasswordReset` silently no-op (anti-enumeration 200, no token, no log), with no way to discover the mismatch from outside.

## Fix

input.description:
## Found by

MM-241 return-leg pre-flight (production → bsky.social). bsky rejected a **provably valid** ES256 service-auth token (`InvalidToken: Token could not be verified`) — our post-MM-304 verifier, resolving the DID's current key fresh from plc.directory, accepts the same token completely. Root cause on bsky's side is almost certainly a stale DID-doc cache. Investigating whether *we* have the same bug: **we do, three ways.**

## Evidence (did:plc:u7j7xdhvkwx3xlf6xjkbpdn7, 2026-07-12, after two same-day PLC ops)

1. plc.directory current `verificationMethods.atproto` = `zDnaepBn1v6…` (production's key). Production's `resolveDid` still serves `zDnaeUWgDx…` — the **staging-era key**, cached at migration `createAccount` time and never updated after the identity leg rewrote the PLC doc.
2. `POST com.atproto.identity.refreshIdentity` for the DID returns the **same stale document** — the "force revalidation" endpoint doesn't actually refresh.
3. `identity_resolution::resolve_did_document` is cache-first with no bypass (`if let Some(doc) = get_did_document(...) { return ... }`) — and it's what `create_account_migration` uses to obtain the `#atproto` key for service-auth JWT verification.

## Consequence

Any DID this server has EVER cached verifies against the fossil key: a migrate-away-and-return account's `createAccount` service token is rejected exactly as bsky rejected ours. Tonight's two successful hops worked only because each destination was cache-cold for the DID. Also: `resolveDid`/`resolveIdentity` serve stale docs to anyone resolving through us, and the cached `alsoKnownAs`/endpoint go stale the same way.

## Fix (reference-parity behavior)

1. Add a force-refresh path to `resolve_did_document` (fetch from PLC / did:web and **rewrite the cache row** on success).
2. `refreshIdentity` uses it (that's the endpoint's entire spec: purge caches, re-resolve, return the fresh view).
3. `verify_service_auth_jwt` call sites (migration `createAccount`): resolve cached → on **signature verification failure only**, force-refresh and retry once — the reference's documented `verifyServiceJwt` behavior. Bounded: one refetch per failed verification, so it's not a DoS-able amplifier (and the existing per-endpoint rate limit covers the route).
4. Consider refreshing own-account docs on `#identity`-adjacent events (activateAccount after migration) so the common case never serves stale.

Tests: seed a stale cached doc + newer PLC mock → migration createAccount succeeds via retry; refreshIdentity rewrites the row; resolveDid serves the new doc after refresh.

Everything's recorded. Where the return leg stands:

**The verdict is clean: our side is provably correct, bsky's side is rejecting.** Your production-minted token verified perfectly against an atproto-conformant verifier resolving the DID's *current* key from plc.directory — signature, curve, claims, expiry, everything. bsky's `InvalidToken` means they're checking against a stale view of your DID (two PLC ops in one day is exactly the scenario that outruns a lazy cache) — or masking an inbound-migration policy refusal. Their auth-gated `reserveSigningKey` and the phone-verification wall suggest the entryway was never made hospitable to walk-ins, which is, notably, *the thesis of this whole product expressed as an error code*.

The investigation paid for itself twice over, though — chasing their bug found **ours**: [MM-310](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-310/did-doc-cache-never-refreshes-custos-verifies-inbound-migrations) (High). Custos's `resolve_did_document` is cache-first with no refresh path, `refreshIdentity` is demonstrably a no-op (I called it against production; the fossil doc came straight back), and since the migration verifier uses that same resolution, **an account migrating back to a Custos that had ever seen it before would be rejected exactly the way bsky rejected us.** Both hops tonight succeeded only because the destinations were cache-cold. The ticket has the reference-parity fix spec (force-refresh path, real `refreshIdentity`, retry-once-on-signature-failure in the verifier).

The plan on [MM-241](https://linear.app/atbb/issue/MM-241): retry the authenticated probe in ~24h — if it's their cache TTL, it heals itself and the return leg is back on. If it's still walled, the return-leg validation moves to a **self-hosted reference PDS** as destination, which proves every seam that's ours to prove (a reference-implementation verifier accepting our ES256 token, reference `importRepo`/blob intake), and bsky.social's posture gets recorded as a finding rather than a failure.

Meanwhile the identity sits happily on production — keys sovereign through three PLC ops, two live hops verified. Whenever you pick this back up: MM-310 is the one to land first if the next move is any migration *into* a warm Custos; the 24h bsky retry is a single curl away. Solid night's work.

input.title: Config enum values are case-sensitive — EZPDS_EMAIL_PROVIDER=SMTP crashes startup
input.description:
## Problem

`EZPDS_EMAIL_PROVIDER=SMTP` (all-caps) fails config validation and aborts startup — the provider match in `crates/pds/src/email.rs` (`sender_from_config`) accepts only the exact lowercase strings `"log"` / `"smtp"`. Env-var values are conventionally written in caps, so this is an easy operator trap: the service crash-loops on deploy over pure letter case.

## Fix

- Normalize enum-valued config strings case-insensitively (`value.trim().to_ascii_lowercase()`) before matching. Audit ALL enum-valued config keys, not just email provider — at minimum: `email.provider`, `[telemetry] log_format` (`"json"`), and any boolean-ish envs parsed by string match.
- Keep unknown values a hard, *descriptive* config error (naming the accepted values) — the crash-on-invalid posture is right; the case-sensitivity is not.
- Tests: uppercase/mixed-case values accepted for each enum key; genuinely unknown value still fails with the enumerated-options message.

Observed live while configuring SMTP on a deployment (2026-07-12, MM-241 aftermath).

input.title: Create-flow OAuth login UX — no username autofill (login_hint never passed) and iOS auto-capitalization breaks sign-in
input.description:
## Problem (user-observed, on device)

During the create flow's first OAuth (the `authenticating` step after handle registration), the in-app authorize page:
1. **Doesn't prefill the username** — even though the wallet literally just registered the handle two screens earlier.
2. **iOS auto-capitalizes the first letter** of the identifier, and the login then fails — annoying and mysterious to a user (the failure gives no hint that case was the problem).

## Root causes

1. The `login_hint` plumbing **already exists end-to-end and is simply not fed**: the authorize template renders `login_hint` into the identifier field (`oauth_templates.rs` — `value="{login_hint}"`, `autocomplete="username"`), `CustosClient::par()` forwards a `login_hint`, and `oauth::prepare_oauth_flow` accepts one — but the frontend's `startOAuthFlow` never supplies the handle. Wallet fix: pass the just-registered handle (create flow has it in state) through `startOAuthFlow` → `prepare_oauth_flow`.
2. The authorize page's identifier `<input>` sets no `autocapitalize`/`autocorrect`/`spellcheck` attributes → iOS capitalizes. Server fix (template): `autocapitalize="none" autocorrect="off" spellcheck="false"`.
3. Defense in depth: the authorize login (and `createSession`) should match identifiers **case-insensitively** — handles are stored lowercase, so `Malpercio.…` fails byte-equality today. Lowercase the identifier before handle resolution (emails: MM-308's normalization covers that side).

Three small fixes, two surfaces (wallet + Custos template/login); together they make the first-login step feel intentional instead of hostile.

input.title: Migration source login prefills the DID instead of the handle
input.description:
## Problem (user-observed, on device, MM-241 legs (b)/(c))

The outbound-migration source-login screen prefills the identifier field with the **DID** (`did:plc:…`) rather than the handle — technically valid (createSession accepts DIDs) but strange as a user: you expect to see your name, not your key.

## Root cause pointer

`MigrationSourceAuthScreen` prefills from its `handle` prop and its comment says handle is intended ("Prefill the login identifier with the handle, then let the user edit it to a DID or email…"). So the *supplier* hands it a DID: either `prepare_migration`'s `PreparedMigration.handle` falls back to the DID (likely when the cached DID doc lacks a usable `alsoKnownAs` — related to the MM-300/301 cache-shape history), or the `+page.svelte` wiring passes `identity.did`. Trace which and fix at the source; fall back to the DID only when no handle is known.

Cheap fix; worth batching with the create-flow OAuth UX ticket (login_hint/autocapitalize) as one wallet-polish PR.

input.title: importRepo's first-write-wins guard blocks return migration into a prior residency — MM-241 leg (d) blocker
input.description:
## Found by

MM-241 **leg (d)** (production → staging, the round-trip closer), on device, 2026-07-12: fails at transfer-repo with `REPO_TRANSFER_FAILED`. One step past MM-310's fix (the warm-cache `createAccount` verified fine — that fix is confirmed live).

## Root cause

Two individually-correct designs interact badly:

- **MM-299** made migration-mode `createAccount` resumable: an existing **deactivated** account for the DID re-issues a session instead of 409ing. Leg (d) resumed the leg (b) staging account.
- **`import_repo`** is first-write-wins (`routes/import_repo.rs`): `if write_state.repo_root_cid.is_some()` → `409 Conflict "account already has a repo"` — written for the mid-flight-retry picture (root absent, or import already complete), protecting against a retried/racing call silently overwriting.

Nobody considered a **completed prior residency**: the resumed account still carries leg (b)'s full repo root, so the return migration's import 409s deterministically. Any migrate-away-and-return round trip hits this; the reference ecosystem supports round trips, so this is also a parity gap.

## State note (leg (d) attempt is cleanly retryable)

The resume consumed nothing (no claim code) and changed nothing; staging's account remains deactivated at leg (b)'s root/rev `3mqdcm57v4u22`. In this specific run the incoming repo is **byte-identical** (same rev — no writes happened on production), which suggests the fix's first tier below already unblocks leg (d).

## Fix design

Server (`import_repo`), two tiers:
1. **Idempotent same-root import**: if the parsed CAR's root == the existing `repo_root_cid`, return 200 without rewriting — a retried import (and this leg-(d) case) is a no-op success.
2. **Replace-on-deactivated with optimistic concurrency**: allow a *different* root to replace the existing one while the account is deactivated, making the atomic commit a compare-and-swap against the root observed at precondition time (`UPDATE … WHERE repo_root_cid IS <observed-old-root>`), so the anti-race property the first-write-wins guard provided is preserved (a concurrent import with a different base loses loudly, nothing is silently clobbered). The deactivated state + the service-auth-derived session is the authorization — same trust chain that authorized the resume.
   - Housekeeping: superseded blocks/`block_owners` rows from the old root become unreferenced → existing GC reconciliation covers them; confirm `blob_owners` grace behavior for blobs no longer referenced by the new root.

Wallet (optional hardening, separate ticket if preferred): `transfer_repo_impl` could treat a dest whose `checkAccountStatus` already reconciles with the source head as import-complete and skip — the orchestrator already has `import_reconciles` machinery.

Tests: same-root reimport 200 no-op (replaces the current `reimport_over_existing_repo_returns_409` expectation); different-root replace succeeds while deactivated; CAS loser errors loudly; active account still refused.

Sequence: land → staging auto-deploy → retry leg (d) with the same (unconsumed) claim code and wallet build.

All recorded. Summary of where leg (d) stands:

**The good news inside the failure**: MM-310's fix passed its live trial — the warm-cache `createAccount` on staging (the step that was deterministically doomed two hours ago) verified production's token and resumed the account. The MM-299-resumed leg (b) account still holds its old root, so the 409 is deterministic. Every `com.atproto.*` route a daily driver needs is implemented: server sessions,
createAccount/describeServer, app passwords, email/account management, repo CRUD + applyWrites
+ uploadBlob + importRepo + listMissingBlobs, the full sync surface incl. Sync v1.1 (`#sync`

signing), service proxying to the AppView with read-after-write munging, chat proxy, the full
atproto OAuth provider stack (PAR, DPoP, rotating refresh, revoke, client-metadata resolution,
granular scopes), preferences, invite/signup, and moderation/admin.

**The gaps are validation, not features:**
1. The **live migration round trip** (bsky.social → ezpds and the credible-exit leg, MM-241)
   has never been executed — the runbook exists with a blank execution record. This is the exact
   path a real account takes. Do not move a real account before it passes.
2. **First real OAuth login by the official Bluesky app** is implemented but unproven — the
   interop suite and HTTP tests authenticate with `createSession` passwords, never OAuth/DPoP.
3. **`atproto-proxy` header is honored only for `com.atproto.moderation.*`**, not `app.bsky.*`,
   so `app.bsky.video.*` (routed by the official app with that header) will not reach the video
   service — **posting video from the official app likely fails**. The resolution machinery
   already exists in the moderation branch; generalizing it is the fix.
4. **Operational config, not code:** the default email sender only logs — password reset,
   PLC-op, email-confirm and account-delete tokens go nowhere until `[email] provider = "smtp"`
   is set.

Proven against the live network (interop suite, staging): account provisioning, identity
triple-agreement, repo CRUD with CID match, live firehose observation, CAR export consistency,
PDS→AppView proxy auth, real social interactions, full account lifecycle incl. reaper purge.

1. **Extract the shared record-write preamble.** `delete_record.rs` and `apply_writes.rs`
